1:
The opening verse reads two ways, and Matthew Henry gives both. Taken as it stands it teaches that we are not sufficient of ourselves to think or speak anything wise, all sufficiency being of God — which is how John Gill and John Wesley take it, Gill picturing the marshalling of a man's confused thoughts like an army drawn up for battle. But most, Henry says, read it otherwise: man purposes, and the answer of the tongue is of the Lord. Adam Clarke puts that reading sharply, the counsels being the free offspring of the heart of man and the answer the free volition of God; Charles Ellicott renders the first clause accordingly: to man belong the counsels of the heart. Keil and Delitzsch add a refinement against three grammarians who took the second clause of a favourable hearing: a man does not always find the fitting expression for what he has in mind, so finding it is a gift from above.

The next verses turn on the difference between a man's estimate of himself and God's. Gill takes the self-satisfied man of the second verse for the self-righteous, ignorant of his own impurity and the spirituality of the law. Henry generalises — we are all partial in judging ourselves — and sets against it the unerring balance in which God weighs the spirits. Ellicott draws the conclusion: a clean conscience does not excuse a man in God's sight, so there is the more reason for anxious self-examination, and for praying still against faults that escaped notice. At the next verse Gill and Ellicott press the literal sense of the verb, to roll one's works upon the Lord as a burden too heavy to carry oneself; Delitzsch rejects three ancient versions which made it reveal rather than roll, since the preposition will not bear it, and notes that the works meant are those still to be done.

The hardest verse is the fourth, and the voices divide over whether it teaches a decree of reprobation. Ellicott denies it outright: the words do not mean God created anyone for punishment or predestined him to destruction, only that even the wicked are subservient to his purposes — Pharaoh could not alter God's plans by rebelling, only give occasion to show his power and longsuffering. Delitzsch removes the ground of the question by repointing, so that the verse says God made everything for its own contemplated end rather than for himself, the older rendering leaving the second clause without a proper parallel. Clarke reports the Chaldee, which turns the first clause toward those who obey God. Henry keeps the received sense and makes God first cause and last end, noting that the wicked fight him with the very powers he gave them; Wesley states a sequence, not a decree: men make themselves wicked and God therefore makes them miserable.

A second dispute follows over whose mercy and truth expiate iniquity. Clarke is most emphatic that the Hebrew is not ambiguous: it says He shall atone for iniquity — God, by his mercy in sending his Son and the truth of what he promised through the prophets — not as though a man could atone by his own charity. Gill agrees, denying that alms deeds or fair dealing can purge sin, and refers the mercy and truth to God. Ellicott allows the human sense only as a sign, such qualities purging nothing except as evidence of faith working by love; Wesley makes them a qualification for offering acceptable prayer for pardon. Delitzsch alone takes the phrase for love and faithfulness between men, not the grace and truth of God at all. The rest is brief: Henry instances Esau made to be at peace with Jacob; at the last verse Delitzsch collects the thought in German, Arabic and Latin, insisting that God does not make a man's steps firm but gives them direction.
10:
The first of the king proverbs is read by most voices as a duty rather than a description. John Gill notes that the word behind the divine sentence means divination, and that while some point to the sagacity Solomon showed between the two harlots, such discernment is not found in kings generally — so the verse states what ought to be, not what is. Matthew Henry says the same with a prayer attached: we wish it were always true, and ought to make it our petition for kings and all in authority, but since it is often otherwise the words may be taken as a precept to kings and judges. Charles Ellicott renders the second clause should not transgress, the king being God's representative on earth and dignified by that title in the Psalter; he hears an echo of Solomon's youth, when his highest aspiration was to judge his people righteously. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result by grammar, treating the first line as a noun clause and correcting Jerome and Luther, whose renderings make the proverb assert what it only requires. Adam Clarke stands apart, reading it as fact about a righteous king: though divination itself were brought to bear on his lips to make him punish the innocent and spare the guilty, they would not transgress, so firmly is he attached to God.

On the just weight the interest is in what exactly is being referred to. Clarke thinks the allusion is probably to the standard weights kept in the sanctuary, against which weights in common use were checked, though others take it of the weights merchants carried in their girdles — a possibility he supports by observing that the Chinese take no coin but gold and silver by weight and carry a small steelyard for it. Henry takes both halves as divine appointments — public justice is an ordinance of God, and so is justice in trade, since he taught men the discretion to make scales and weights at all.

The two verses on the good king raise the question whether such a king ever existed. Ellicott is blunt that he did not: this is the ideal, and Israel's history shows how feebly Solomon or the best of his successors fulfilled it, the conception being too high for man and answered only in David's Son. Henry treats it as a character rather than a portrait, offered not for Solomon's own praise but for his successors' instruction, and observes that such a king hates flatterers and is willing that all about him deal faithfully with him whether the truth pleases or displeases. Gill records the contrary as usual, kings hearkening to those who flatter their pride and love of power. Clarke passes over the pair as plain, remarking that these sayings concern monarchical government rightly administered.

The last two verses form a matched pair on the king's power. Henry says they show how great that power was, especially in eastern countries where kings were absolute and their will was law, and adds an aside blessing God for a constitution which maintains the prerogative of the prince without injury to the liberty of the subject. Gill takes the messengers of death for the Targum's angels of death, instances the wrath of Ahasuerus falling on Haman, and explains the plural as one messenger sent after another; Delitzsch agrees it strengthens the figure and gives it a face, the wrinkled brow and flaming eye standing for the troop. Gill turns the light of the countenance toward the King of kings, whose favour and gracious presence are life to his people. Ellicott stays with the agriculture: the latter rain fell at the end of March, maturing the barley and wheat before the April harvest, and was eagerly looked for. Wesley says only that the favour is as acceptable as the clouds which bring that rain.
16:
Matthew Henry notes how the preference of wisdom over gold is stated: not merely asserted but urged with admiration at the disproportion, and with an appeal to the reader's conscience to judge how much better it is. He grounds the difference in giver and beneficiary alike — grace is the gift of God's peculiar favour where gold is of common providence, and grace is for ourselves where gold is for others. John Gill takes the wisdom for Christ, the fountain in whom the treasures are hid. Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of a series on wisdom, righteousness, humility and trust in God, read as a succession of steps, humility being the virtue of virtues and trust in God the condition of all salvation; the striving is commended because such a possession comes by acquisition, not inheritance. Against all this Adam Clarke sets one question: whether anyone believes it, though spoken by the wisest of men under divine inspiration.

The highway of the next verse is described differently by each voice. Henry makes it a public road marked out by authority, tracked by many who went before and shared with company met on the way. Delitzsch makes it a single road, straight and unimpeded, made so by the avoidance of evil which would entice a man aside to right or left. Charles Ellicott calls it the plain way of duty lying in front of a man, which cannot be mistaken whatever his other difficulties. Gill names it the King's highway, the way of holiness in which men, though fools, shall not err. John Wesley alone allows departure from it, calling it their common road though through frailty they slip into the bypath of sin. Clarke puts the verse in one clause: the upright man is ever departing from evil, and by keeping that road preserves his soul.

On pride Clarke offers two personifications, pride walking with destruction in its train and haughtiness marching on with ruin behind; and he records the Masoretic note printed in most Hebrew Bibles here: this is the middle of the book, the middle verse, its first clause ending the middle of its words. Delitzsch collects parallels: a Latin proverb that great things fall, inflated things burst and swollen things are crushed, and a Hebrew play on two accent names in which a rising is followed by a breaking; the noun, he insists, means the fracture of a body, not bursting or shipwreck. Henry presses the certainty of the fall: those who lift themselves up will be brought down by repentance or ruin, and since men cannot punish pride but only admire or fear it, God takes the punishing into his own hands. He adds that proud men are often most insolent just before their destruction. Gill supplies instances, from the fallen angels and our first parents to Haman and Nebuchadnezzar; Ellicott notes the contrast with the blessing promised to humility just before.

The last verse is a paradox, Henry says, which the children of this world will not subscribe to: better to be poor and humble than rich and proud. Those who divide the spoil are commonly proud, their minds rising with their condition, and the men who scramble for preferment are the ones who get it and have the world at will. Gill puts the humble among the followers of the meek and lowly Jesus, with mean thoughts of themselves and resigned to God. Delitzsch takes a textual point that changes the sense: there is no reason to alter the written form of the word to the marginal one, since it may be understood of sufferers as well as of the humble, so that the verse sets the inward fact of humility against the outward act of dividing spoil. The choice is then not between two tempers but two companies, and what is commended is dwelling lowly among the afflicted.
20:
The first verse of this group is read two ways. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott take the object to be the divine word, so the promise belongs to the man who gives heed to it — Delitzsch setting the clause against the despising of the word earlier in the book and making attention to it the way to true prosperity. Matthew Henry and John Wesley keep the practical sense, of a man master of his trade and considerate in his affairs; but Henry adds that prudence only gains repute, and a man who handles matters wisely while leaning on his own understanding finds little satisfaction in the good he gets.

Three verses on wisdom and eloquence follow, and their relation is the question. Delitzsch describes the sweetness of the lips in Cicero's phrase for beauty of speech, of no significance for learning itself but of great value for teaching it. Ellicott says the power to express thought in graceful language adds greatly to learning's value. Henry treats the later verse as a correction: Solomon had commended eloquence and seemed to set it above wisdom, but now shows that unless there is a treasure within to support it, it is worth little, and that however fine the language, what is unseasonable had better be unsaid. On the earlier verse he notes what the eloquent man gains by giving: he diffuses knowledge and thereby increases his own stock, which Wesley puts plainly, that a man improves himself while teaching.

Between them stands the wellspring of life, where Adam Clarke sees another anatomical allusion, to the artery carrying blood from the heart to the extremities. The second half of that verse is disputed. Delitzsch corrects two commentators who took the instruction of fools for the teaching fools give, laying down that when fools are the subject the word always means the training given them. Ellicott sets out both without deciding — either the discipline fools administer is worse than useless, being folly itself, or the discipline they endure is folly, since those who will not be taught by wisdom are corrected by their own foolishness instead. Henry takes the rejected sense: nothing good is to be got from a fool, whose set and solemn discourses are themselves folly.

The honeycomb draws a characteristic note from Clarke, that honey in the comb is sweeter and finer than what has been pressed out and exposed to air. Delitzsch defines the pleasant words as words love suggests and that breathe love, and observes that the healing promised not only restores soundness but preserves and advances it. Henry ties them to the previous verse, so the words commended are those the heart of the wise teaches; Gill applies them to the doctrines of the Gospel, where a Jewish commentator had applied them to the law. The warning that follows is a repetition, as Clarke and Gill note; Gill takes the repetition as the point, the observation being important enough to demand attention twice, and Henry reads it both as caution against self-deception and as terror to the man whose way is wrong however right it looks.

The last verse turns on who is doing the labouring. Our version has the man labouring for himself, which Gill accepts while remarking that one who labours to grow rich lays up more for others than himself; Clarke states it bluntly, that no thanks are due a man for his industry, since if he does not work he must starve. Ellicott and Delitzsch read the Hebrew differently, making the labourer's hunger what labours for him and his mouth what urges him on, so that the strength for the work comes from knowing it supplies his need. Henry takes another route from the same words, reading the soul as the labourer and applying it all to heart-work, since the mouth's continual craving means a man must either work or starve.
27:
Four portraits of bad men open the passage, and Matthew Henry sorts them in two — those who envy a man his good name and dig up evil to blast it; and those who, like Satan, work by force as roaring lions rather than by fraud as subtle serpents. John Gill takes the first for a man of Belial, without a yoke, who digs for sin as for treasure and need not go far, having enough in his own heart; he supplies two instances from church history, one party raking up an early father's youthful sins and another serving Beza so. Adam Clarke compares the labour to quarrying, a wicked man working as hard at an evil purpose as a quarryman at stones; the burning lips he explains as words igniting strife as fire does dry stubble. Charles Ellicott and John Wesley refer the phrase to the tongue set on fire of hell.

Keil and Delitzsch handle the next two philologically. The whisperer is named from a root meaning to murmur; and the violent man's enticement is not moral seduction but enticement to a place which makes the intended violence practicable, the noun for violence meaning the injustice of club-law, of a man who puts his own force in the place of God. On the closing gesture Delitzsch offers what he calls a warning in physiognomy: biting the lips is the act of the deceitful and denotes scorn and knavery, and the tense implies that a man seen doing it has the evil as good as done. Clarke and Wesley read the shut eyes as concentration, closing out every other idea so the whole soul may be in this; Gill adds that such a man shuts his eyes against the light of Scripture lest his practices be reproved.

The hoary head raises a real question of grammar. Our version makes the crown conditional, and Henry takes it so, urging that it ought to be the great care of old people to be found in the way of righteousness, since God and man will look for them there. Ellicott corrects the conditional to a statement, the crown being found in the way of righteousness because long life is itself promised as the reward of obedience. Delitzsch holds both together, treating length of days as on one side a natural consequence and on another a promised recompense.

On the man slow to anger, Clarke is fullest: it is easier to subdue an enemy without than one within, and many kings who conquered nations were slaves to their own passions — Alexander, who conquered the world, killing Clytus, the closest of his friends, in a fit of intemperate anger. He notes that most nations have coined a similar proverb, quoting one from Horace. Ellicott says only that victory over self is the hardest of victories.

The lot closes the chapter, and the question is whether it may still be used. Henry states the principle: nothing comes to pass by chance, and what man has neither eye nor hand in, God is concerned in; such appeals must eye God by prayer. Gill allows the practice but hedges it: never in trivial cases, nor for curiosity or gain, nor rashly, but seriously and religiously, with prayer and in faith. Clarke will not say how far it is proper now, granting it was once lawful and efficient, the decision being taken as from the Lord immediately, and is still allowed even by writers on civil law — but he adds that those who most need recourse to it are those with neither piety to pray nor faith to trust God for an answer. Delitzsch notes that the law ordains the lot nowhere, knowing only one ordeal, its use resting on a custom running parallel to the law. Ellicott draws the encouragement: much we attribute to chance is due to the providence of God.
